## Observations

1. An operation centered at position \(j\) requires \(S_j\) to be `R` and its two neighbors to be `A` and `C` in either order. It sets \(A_{j-1}\) and \(A_j\) to 1. Since operations do not change the string, only the set of centers used matters.
2. Let \(x_i\) indicate whether position \(i\) is a chosen center. Adjacent positions cannot both be centers, because a center needs non-`R` neighbors. Also, every initial zero \(A_i\) requires at least one of \(x_i\) and \(x_{i+1}\) to be 1, with indices taken cyclically.
3. For any choice of nonadjacent centers, keep the two edges incident to each chosen center in the position cycle. If any edge is missing, the resulting components are paths or isolated vertices. On each path, assign `R` to the centers and alternate `A` and `C` among the other vertices; this gives every chosen center the required neighbors.
4. No edge is missing exactly when the center bits alternate around the entire cycle. In that case, the \(N/2\) noncenter letters must alternate between `A` and `C` cyclically, which is possible exactly when \(N\) is divisible by 4.
5. After fixing \(x_1\), the checks can be done with a constant-size state: the most recent center bit and a flag indicating whether a pair of consecutive zero center bits has been seen. Such a pair marks a missing edge.

## Solution sketch

1. “An operation centered at position \(j\) requires \(S_j\) to be `R` and its two neighbors to be `A` and `C` in either order. It sets \(A_{j-1}\) and \(A_j\) to 1. Since operations do not change the string, only the set of centers used matters.” Search for a feasible choice of center bits rather than constructing a string or simulating operations. If the input has no zeros, print `Yes` immediately: no operations are needed.
2. “Adjacent positions cannot both be centers, because a center needs non-`R` neighbors. Also, every initial zero \(A_i\) requires at least one of \(x_i\) and \(x_{i+1}\) to be 1, with indices taken cyclically.” For each possible value of \(x_1\), start a dynamic program with that bit and the missing-edge flag unset. For each \(i\) from \(1\) through \(N-1\), try both values of \(x_{i+1}\) from every reachable state. Reject a pair if both bits are 1, or if both bits are 0 and \(A_i=0\). Otherwise, keep the new bit and set the flag if the pair is \(0,0\).
3. “If any edge is missing, the resulting components are paths or isolated vertices.” Close the cycle by checking \((x_N,x_1)\) against the same rules using \(A_N\), and update the flag for this final pair as well. If a state passes the closing check and the flag is set, print `Yes`: the path assignments from Observation 3 make all chosen centers usable.
4. “In that case, the \(N/2\) noncenter letters must alternate between `A` and `C` cyclically, which is possible exactly when \(N\) is divisible by 4.” If a state passes the closing check but its flag is unset, accept it only when \(N\) is divisible by 4. Print `No` if neither starting bit yields an accepted state. This also handles odd \(N\): a fully alternating choice cannot pass all the cyclic pair checks.
5. “After fixing \(x_1\), the checks can be done with a constant-size state: the most recent center bit and a flag indicating whether a pair of consecutive zero center bits has been seen.” Keep only the current and next sets of reachable states. The two runs take \(O(N)\) time and \(O(1)\) auxiliary space beyond the \(O(N)\) stored input.
